title: US Medicaid nursing-home financing can reward volume over quality and shift patients toward worse providers
source_unit: US Medicaid nursing-home financing, federal matching grants, state creative financing, dementia admissions, facility quality, and one-year survival
geography: United States; 24 federal audits and Indiana administrative microdata

observations.period: Working paper issued August 2025; US Medicaid and Indiana administrative evidence

denominator.unit: federal audits used alongside Indiana administrative microdata

financing_incentive.unit: federal matching grants reward verifiable nursing-home volume rather than measured quality

dementia_volume.unit: percent increase in Medicaid dementia volume in event-study estimates

facility_quality.unit: the expansion concentrates in the lowest-quality facilities

patient_allocation.unit: patients are reallocated toward worse providers

one_year_survival.unit: one-year survival falls after the expansion

public_moral_hazard.unit: state creative financing diverts funds earmarked for nursing homes and turns the federal match into a volume subsidy

observations.method: The paper develops a theoretical mechanism and tests its predictions using 24 federal audits, administrative microdata from Indiana, event studies, and structural quality estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose the full sample counts, effect sizes beyond the 12% volume estimate, the exact survival estimates, or all identification assumptions. Indiana evidence and federal audits may not generalize to every state; the paper does not measure worker conditions, resident voice, prices, or every form of Medicaid financing.
observations.subgroup: Medicaid dementia patients and nursing-home facilities, especially lower-quality providers exposed to the financing expansion.
observations.counterinterpretation: Measured quality, admissions, and survival may reflect selection, coding, facility capacity, patient severity, state administration, or concurrent policy changes; the volume response does not by itself identify the full fiscal or clinical mechanism outside the studied setting.

related_sources.claim: Nursing-home financial evidence reports related-party profit tunneling and a large gap between reported and adjusted investment returns.
Nursing-home mergers reduce deficiency citations and direct-care hours without meaningful resident-health improvement.
Inspection responses are mostly temporary, while higher ratings predict relative patient mortality.

boundary: This record adds a Medicaid payment-design and patient-allocation layer to the US nursing-home chain. It does not establish that every matching grant causes harm, disclose all effect sizes, or measure worker outcomes, resident voice, prices, access, or long-run care quality in one common unit.
